In the updated version of Figure 5a, we included additional experiments in DU145 and PC3 cell lines to demonstrate that, similar to colorectal cancer cells, eIF5A is associated with MYC mRNA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that GC7 slightly decreased c-MYC expression but to a less extend than MRPP3 MRPP3 (Ext Data Fig. 8a). Interestingly, leptomycin B an inhibitor of Exportin 1 (XPO1) that participates in the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic transport of MYC mRNA in hepatocarcinoma cells (Deutzman et al. 2024) also slightly inhibited c-MYC expression in PCa cells. Yes, MYC is overexpressed in prostate cancer and we now mention in the discussion that MYC plays an important role in this cancer. 11/ The authors clearly showed that hypusination regulates MRPP3 translation. When they overexpress the gene encoding for MRPP3, the phenotype associated with DHPS silencing is reversed. However, if DHPS is knockdown, the level of MRPP3 protein should be still low since the machinery for its translation is reduced, even if the gene is more expressed. Do the authors think that overexpressing a gene can counteract a reduction of hypusination? Please, show MRPP3 protein levels in the tumors of the different groups. ANSWER: The reviewer's insightful remark is correct. Indeed, we observed that under conditions where MRPP3 is overexpressed, the inhibition of hypusination (either by GC7 or shDHPS) reduces MRPP3 expression. However, this reduction remains higher in cells treated with GC7 or shDHPS alone (Fig. 4g and Extended data Fig. 7d, 9j, 10a,d). So, the translation machinery may be inhibited but not sufficiently to counteract MRPP3 mRNA gene overexpression. We have added the expression of MRPP3 in the mice tumors (New Ext Data Fig. 10a). 12/ The paper would be greatly improved using a syngeneic model of prostate cancer. ANSWER: The reviewer is right, the demonstration of the role of eIF5A hypusinated in a syngeneic model reinforces our conclusion. Thus, we performed in vivo experiments doing allograft injection of RM-1 cells (ATCC ref# CRL-3310) a murine prostate cancer cell line in C57Bl6J immunocompetent mice. RM-1 have been previously used in vivo in several studies, for example by Zhou et al. (PMID: 38569039), Chen et al. (PMID: 30841425), Liu et al. (PMID: 36046655), Xu et al. (PMID : 30841931), Yang et al. (PMID : 39127402) or Krzastek et al. (PMID : 29943070). Using this syngeneic model, we did an experiment with GC7, with RM-1 cells expressing shDHPS, RM-1 cells expressing shMRPP3 and a rescue experiment with MRPP3 expressing plasmid. We demonstrated that the treatment with GC7 as well as the downregulation of DHPS or MRPP3 inhibit tumor growth, furthermore, we confirmed that MRPP3 overexpression counteracted partially the anti-tumoral effects resulting from the downregulation of DHPS in the RM-1 syngeneic model (Fig. 2f, Fig. 6e, Ext Data Fig. 4g,h 10b-d). Minor comments: 13/ The scheme of biosynthesis of EIF5A-Hyp in Fig. 1a is not accurate. DHPS uses spermidine and the Lys50 of EIF5A as substrate. Same remark for Extended Data Fig. 2b. ANSWER: The reviewer is right and we have corrected the scheme in the new version of Fig. 1a., we also modified the scheme in Extended Data Fig.3a (previously 2b). 14/ In the abstract and Introduction (lines 47 and 68), put the abbreviation in parenthesis after the complete name of the protein. ANSWER: We did the modifications accordingly. 15/ In general, remove the P value from the text since they are shown in the figures. ANSWER: We removed the p value in the text when they are indicated in the figures. 16/ Line 939: do not capitalize Primary. ANSWER: The change is done. 17/ Please, describe the epidemiology, etiology, and disease progression of prostate cancer as a first paragraph of the introduction. ANSWER: As requested we added a paragraph on PCa in the introduction: “According to the GLOBOCAN study, PCa is the second most diagnosed cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer death among men worldwide {Bray, 2024 #3269}. Removal of the prostate (prostatectomy) and radiotherapy are treatments for localized tumors. For more advanced PCa, anti-androgen treatments and/or chemotherapy (Docetaxel) are prescribed. However, patients quickly develop resistance, leading to fatal outcomes. Therefore, there is a critical need to discover therapies that target new molecular pathways.” 18/ Fig. 1h should appear before Fig. 1e, since it is a transcriptomic analysis. ANSWER: We did the modifications accordingly. 19/ Describe more specifically Fig. 2a in the Results section. Why the authors did not use a western blot? At which time point was performed the analysis of EIF5A-hyp level? ANSWER: The reviewer is right, we did not comment this figure in the results, thus, we added a sentence in the new version of the manuscript. In addition to cytometry analysis, we present in the new version immunoblots of the expression of eIF5A hypusinated and DHPS in the tumoroids. We added this new sentence to the results section: “We verified by cytometry and immunoblot that both GC7 and the downregulation of DHPS decreased eIF5Ahyp (Fig. 2a, Extended Data Fig. 3f,g).”. However, we must emphasize that tumoroids are 3D structures; thus, analysis using Western blotting will average the signal, unlike cytometry, which performs individual cell analysis. Furthermore, we need a lot of tumoroids to obtain a sufficient amount of protein to perform a Western blot. The levels of eIF5Ahyp were analyzed 24 hours after the addition of GC7 and 6 days after the addition of IPTG for shDHPS. This information has been added to the Materials and Methods section: “Tumoroids were treated 24 hours with 80µM GC7 or 6 days with 500µM IPTG to induce the shDHPS before cytometry analysis.” 20/ The legend of Fig. 6f needs revision. ANSWER: We have re-written the legend of the figure 6 f in the new version: “DU145 cells expressing shCtl or shDHPS were stably transfected with empty vector (EV) or MRPP3 expressing plasmid and subcutaneously injected in nude mice (n=8 per group). Graphs represent the follow-up of the tumor volume and the tumor weight. Pictures of the tumors from the four cell lines are taken at the end of the experiment.” 21/ Fig. 5b should be included in the Extended Data. It is already known that hypusination is required for nuclear translocation. ANSWER: We agree with the reviewer that it is known that hypusination is required for nuclear translocation, however, we think that it is important to show these results in the main figures, because it is the main mechanisms explaining how eIF5A regulates MRPP3 expression. 22/ In Fig. 6f, I suggest writing ‘EV + shCtl’, ‘MRPP3 + shDHPS’, etc… instead of ‘EV shCtl’, ‘MRPP3 shDHPS’, etc… ANSWER: As requested by the reviewer, we did the modifications in the new Figure 6. 23/ The last paragraph of the Discussion should be developed. Define RBP. What are the clinical implications of their discovery about the essential role of hypusination in prostate cancer. ANSWER: In the new version of the manuscript, we defined RBP and added the following paragraph: “In conclusion, our results reveal that the RBP (RNA binding protein) function of eIF5A controls MRPP3 expression and PCa metastasis. This provides a new molecular basis for developing novel therapies targeting mitochondrial function in advanced PCa, for which few therapeutic options are available.” 24/ Include a paragraph about Statistics in the Methods section ANSWER: Thanks for this suggestion, we added the following paragraph: “All experiments were performed at least three independent times unless stated. Statistical analyses were performed with GaphPad Prism version 9.0 using appropriate test: Student’s t test, Mann-Whitney or ANOVA.” REVIEWER # 2 We would like to thank the Reviewer for their careful review of our manuscript and for their positive feedback, stating that "Overall, the paper is well written, the story is original, and it is supported by several elegant and solid experimental approaches." We have taken the constructive suggestions into consideration to improve our manuscript and hope that the revisions will meet her/his expectations. Below are our answers: - In very recent Nature paper from the Fendt group (DOI https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08335-7) it was shown that hypusinated EIF5A regulates cancer metastasis in response to aspartate content in the TME. By stimulating NMDA receptors, asp was shown to increase intracellular calcium content, leading to CREB-mediated induction of DOHH transcription, increased EIF5A hypusination and consequent translation of TGFbeta targets involved in metastasis. It would be worth to try to connect the present findings with those from the Fendt group. Is the mechanism described here only applicable to prostate cancer? Are there potential overlapping steps? ANSWER: We thank the reviewer for mentioning this interesting paper published in Nature after the submission of our manuscript (Doglioni et al. January 2025). This article demonstrates that aspartate triggers a molecular cascade that activates CREB, which in turn induces the expression of DOHH mRNA and protein. The increased expression of DOHH enhances hypusination, thereby promoting lung metastasis. Doglioni et al. also demonstrated that Aspartate promotes the N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor activity and this is required for DOHH expression in breast cancer cells metastasis. We analyzed the expression of DOHH and GRIN2D (encoding for NMDA) mRNA and we found no significant modification of their expression in primary tumors (PT) vs metastasis (META) in our PCa orthotopic model (Data for reviewers only below). This result has been added to the new version of the manuscript in the discussion: “More recently, Doglioni et al. demonstrated that Aspartate promotes the N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor activity, and this is required for DOHH mRNA expression in breast cancer cells metastasis. We analyzed the expression of DOHH and NMDA (Grin2d) in primary tumors and the metastasis of PCa orthotopic xenografts and did not find significant changes in mRNA expression (Data shown) suggesting that this mechanism may not be implicated in PCa.” - Figure 1: there are two members of EIF5A proteins: EIF5A1 and EIF5A2. Since previous studies have shown that EIF5A2 is upregulated in some cancers and involved in metastasis, including prostate cancer metastasis (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41420-021-00764-x ), analysis of EIF5A2 should be conducted along with that of EIF5A1. Also, please normalize the levels of hypEIF5A to total EIF5A rather than ERK2 and show the OS also for EIF5A1 and 2. ANSWER: This is an issue also raised by Reviewer #1, we have added the expression data for eIF5A and eIF5A2 to Figure 1B and other analysis included the data obtained with both isoforms in the new Fig.1b, Ext Data Fig. 1d-j., Ext Data Fig. 2a-d. Consistent with previous findings (Clement et al., 2006, PMID: 16519677), we confirm that eIF5A2 is very weakly expressed in prostate cancer cells. Additionally, we have included a sentence in the introduction discussing the two isoforms of eIF5A. We thank the reviewer for bringing to our attention the study by Zheng et al. It is important to note that this study used an antibody that was marketed at the time as specific for eIF5A2. After the publication of this study the supplier posted this note : “This product was previously published with the name Anti-eIF5A2 antibody [EPR7411-6]. Following in-house testing that showed reactivity to both recombinant Human eIF5A protein (ab87457) and recombinant Human eIF5A2 protein (ab99140), the name was updated in January 2021 to Anti-eIF5A2 + eIF5A antibody [EPR7411-6]. Consequently, the specificity of this antibody for eIF5A2 is not guaranteed. Nevertheless, the findings of the publication align with our current manuscript, demonstrating that eIF5A plays an important role in prostate cancer.” In the new Figure 1j the expression of eIF5Ahyp has been normalized to eIF5A . - Figure 2: can the authors provide evidence of the effect of DHPS inhibition on cell proliferation (i.e. BrDU staining or cell proliferation rate) in their cell lines? In addition, since in figure 2g it is difficult to visualize the metastases quantified in Figure 2h (same also in Figs 6g and 6h), can the authors show the luminescence on the explanted organs? ANSWER: As requested by the reviewer the effects of DHPS inhibition (with GC7 and shDHPS) on LNCaP, DU145 and PC3 proliferation were added to the new version of the manuscript (Extended Data Fig. 3 b,c). We have included the luminescence of the organs from the mice injected with ShCT, shDHPS and shMRPP3 in the new version of the manuscript (Extended Data Fig. 4j and Extended Fig. 10e). - Figure 3: can the authors show the whole list of the 71 metabolites identified by MS in a table? ANSWER: We added a new table (Table 2) with the list of the 71 metabolites modified upon the downregulation of DHPS as requested by the reviewer. - Figure 4: Most of the experiments in this figure are conducted with GC7. A previous paper from the Kahana group (DOI 10.1074/jbc.M110.106419) showed different polysomal profiles in response to GC7 (inhibition of initiation) compared to EIF5A knockdown (inhibition of elongation). This should be addressed. Also, a table with the list of proteins identified by MS would be helpful. ANSWER: The reviewer pointed out a paper published in JBC in 2010 demonstrating that GC7 inhibits eIF5A initiation and elongation whereas depletion of eIF5A inhibits elongation only (Landau et al. 2010). We addressed this question in the discussion: “Studies conducted by Kahana's group revealed that GC7 inhibits both initiation and elongation, whereas shRNA targeting eIF5A specifically inhibits elongation {Landau, 2010 #3273}. This discrepancy may be due to the off-target effects of GC7. However, eIF5A has been involved in all stages of translation. It regulates initiation {Ivanov, 2018 #3275} and more specifically the fidelity of star codon initiation {Manjunath, 2019 #3210}, but it also plays a crucial role in the elongation and termination phases {Schuller, 2017 #3086; Pelechano, 2017 #2848}. In our study, we downregulated DHPS and utilized GC7. Notably, both interventions exhibited similar effects on PCa cells and tumor growth, and they similarly influenced MRPP3 expression, minimizing potential but still possible off-target effects of GC7.” The list of proteins identified by MS are available on PRIDE (accession number PXD058627) as indicated in the new version of the manuscript. We also included the accession number for the RNA Seq in the material and method section. - Figure 5: GC7 treatment is shown to increase the nuclear enrichment of MRPP3 and C-MYC, suggesting that hypusination may regulate their shuttling. However, while MRPP3 mRNA is shown to associate with EIF5A, MYC mRNA seems to be slightly enriched although not significantly. This result is somehow puzzling, authors may increase the number of replicates in Fig. 5a to see if statistical significance can be reached or delete the C-MYC data or provide an explanation for the observed discrepancy. Is C-MYC content regulated by GC7 as previously shown (doi: 10.1038/s41419-020-03174-6)? In response to the reviewer comments, we increased the number of replicates in Figure 5a and we performed the experiment in additional PCa cell line (PC3). We demonstrated that in both DU145 and PC3 c-MYC mRNA associated with eIF5A (New figure 5a), consequently, we observed a slight inhibition of c-MYC protein levels in cells treated with GC7 (Ext Data Fig. 8a). - A graphical abstract would be helpful. ANSWER: Thanks for the suggestion. We added a graphical abstract to the revised version of the manuscript (Fig. 7). REVIEWER # 3 The reviewer 3 co-reviewed the article with another reviewer as part of the Early Career Researchers program. REVIEWER #4 We thank the reviewer for carefully reading our manuscript and for the constructive comments made. One of the major concerns was the clinical relevance of our work for the pathology of PCa: “ The main concern is the lack of a proper interrogation of the human relevance of this axis in PCa in the context of the current knowledge. There is no clear identification of which prostate tumors depend on eIF5A and are, therefore, vulnerable to the inhibition of this pathway. Is eIF5A-hyp relevant in primary PCa, or in CRPC? Is it more critical just in metastasis?” Thanks to this suggestion, we have strengthened this issue in the new version of the manuscript by conducting in-depth analysis on previously analyzed databases, but also new databases including proteomic data and neuroendocrine PCa. Our analysis demonstrates that it is primarily the expression of DHPS that increases during PCa progression and metastasis. Additionally, we would like to emphasize that the polyamine-hypusination axis is highly relevant, particularly since the prostate is one of the organs with the highest concentrations of polyamines. This point is addressed in both the introduction and discussion sections of the article: “Polyamines play an important role in cell proliferation, apoptosis, protein and nucleotide synthesis{Casero, 2018 #2634}. Previous studies, including our own, have demonstrated that polyamines are essential for metastasis in PCa (Kaminski et al., 2019; Zabala-Letona et al., 2017), and their levels are significantly elevated in PCa tissues compared to benign prostatic hyperplasia or normal prostate tissues (Zabala-Letona et al., 2017). These findings point to the polyamine/hypusination axis as a central player in PCa progression.”. “Since polyamines are elevated in prostate (Devens et al, 2000 #2829) the study of hypusination is highly relevant.” Below are our answers to the specific points raised by the reviewer: Specific points: Important Note: As requested by the reviewer 1 and 2 we have analyzed the expression of EIF5A and EIF5A2 and we added a paragraph on these two isoforms in the introduction: “There are two known highly homologous (91%) isoforms of eIF5A: eIF5A1 and eIF5A2 encoded by two different genes located on two different chromosomes. However, eIF5A2 expression is weak in the prostate {Clement, 2006 #3162}.” Fig. 1 and Extended Fig. 1. The data of these Figures show the expression of different components of the eIF5A hypusination pathway using several public datasets but in a scattered manner, independently analyzing different components in each dataset. Is there a correlation between DHPS, EIF5A and DOHH mRNA levels in the datasets of Figs. 1b, 1h and Ext Fig. 1c (TCGA)? ANSWER: We performed correlation analysis for DHPS, DOHH, EIF5A and EIF5A2 mRNA using the databases TCGA, Lapointe, Grasso and Varambilly as requested by the reviewer and the conclusion is included in the results section : “In TCGA and Grasso databases, a correlation was observed between eIF5A, DHPS and DOHH expression (Extended Data Fig. 1j), however, eIF5A and DOHH were not significantly associated with PCa (Extended Data Fig.1g-i).”. Of note, we also performed a correlation analysis with the Sun proteomic database and we found that the expression of eIF5A, DHPS and DOOH are significantly correlated (Extended Fig. 7b). How is the expression of EIF5A and DOHH in Fig. 1h? Overall, the paper is well written, the story is original and supported by several elegant and solid experimental approaches.” (Reviewer #2, 3). Furthermore, while we acknowledge that the immunoblots of the patient samples are not perfect, we are certainly willing to provide higher-quality images if required to meet the publication standards. Nice, December 9th, 2025 Answer to the reviewer: Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author): “I thank the authors for their thorough and thoughtful response to my previous critique and appreciate the considerable effort they have devoted to strengthening the manuscript. The additional analyses addressing AR signaling, including the lack of correlation between AR activity and hypusination pathway gene expression, and the demonstration that eIF5Ahyp inhibition does not alter AR levels or activity, help to clarify the AR-independence of the hypusination axis. These additions enhance both the mechanistic depth and clinical relevance of the study. I appreciate the authors’ responsiveness and support the publication of the revised manuscript in Nature Communications. Further improvement in the quality of the western blot images would enhance the overall clarity and presentation of the findings.” ANSWER: We sincerely thank Reviewer #4 for their supportive remark regarding the publication of our revised manuscript in Nature Communications. In response, we have enhanced the quality of the Western blot images to the highest possible standard and hope that these improvements are satisfactory. Dr Frédéric Bost

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have responded very precisely to each of my critics. The paper is clearer, very strong, and greatly improved by the syngeneic model. My initial enthusiasm has been strengthen by this revised submission.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have provided thorough and satisfactory responses to all comments. The revisions have substantially improved the manuscript, which is now suitable for publication.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: I thank the authors for their efforts during the revision to address my previous comments, and I appreciate the additional experiments and new analyses included in the revised manuscript. However, most of my major concerns remain only partially (at most) addressed. As I mentioned in my previous review, the paper falls short in identifying which prostate tumors depend on eIF5Ahyp and in linking the response to targeting this pathway, either pharmacologically with inhibitors or through genetic manipulation with shRNA, to specific patterns of expression or dependencies. Although the revised version includes expanded expression analyses from TCGA and other public datasets, including neuroendocrine PCa, the new data do not provide a cohesive picture of the human relevance of the eiF5Ahyp axis or its expression across different stages or subtypes of PCa. The expression and dependency of this pathway in primary versus metastatic disease, AR-positive versus AR-negative tumors, or castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) remain largely unexplored, and the results differ among the datasets analyzed, precluding reaching more definitive conclusions. It is still unclear what drives the increase in eiF5Ahyp and at what level (mRNA, protein, which step, in which stage?). The results from the different datasets and cohorts are scattered, superficially analyzed, and contradictory among them. The analysis of the scRNAseq dataset does not add any information. The UMAPs shown without splitting by normal or tumor do not demonstrate that the pathway is increased in tumor samples. The responses of the authors to address the contradictory results presented do not solve these problems. Similar inconsistencies are seen with the different model systems used in the study (cell lines and prostate tumoroids). First, the data are not robust enough across experiments, and there are still multiple discrepancies. For example, LNCaP cells show similar levels of eiF5Ahyp compared to normal prostate cells (P69) and lower than DU145 or PC3 (at least in the blots with GC7, Ext Fig. 3a). However, they respond to most of the proliferation, migration, and invasion assays better or at least as well (Ext. Fig.3b). Additionally, although normal controls (P69 and normal organoids) have been included for expression analysis and in one experiment for sensitivity to GC7, most experiments do not include controls run in parallel to demonstrate selectivity. While the inclusion of normal prostate organoids as controls for GC7 sensitivity is valuable, a detailed quantification of eIF5Ahyp and DHPS levels across the different PCa subtypes and correlation with sensitivity to GC7 or shDHPS is still missing. Significant discrepancies persist in mitochondrial functional assays across models. The revised manuscript includes new polysome profiling and proteomic data, which add weight to the involvement of eIF5Ahyp in mitochondrial function. Nevertheless, the identification of MRPP3 as the primary downstream mediator remains speculative, and the revised version has not provided a stronger rationale. The data do not strongly support, in a robust manner, that MRPP3 is the main target downstream of eIF5Ahyp. Significant discrepancies persist in mitochondrial functional assays across different models. For instance, oxygen consumption rate phenotypes upon DHPS and MRPP3 depletion are not fully aligned, raising concerns about the consistency of the proposed mechanism. Likewise, there is no correlation between levels of MRPP3 in the different models and the response to shDHPS or GC7 treatments (see Ext. Fig. 7c and Fig.2b as examples, equal reduction in MRPP3 by shDHPS in all tumorids, but different effect on tumor size). More importantly, the correlation of MRPP3 protein expression with eIF5Ahyp or DHPS levels in human PCa samples is not provided, which reduces the human relevance of the reported findings. The quality of the data, particularly immunoblots and immunofluorescence images, remains suboptimal. In summary, despite the revision, the manuscript at this stage still does not provide a significant advance for the PCa field, and it does not meet the expected rigor and quality for publication in Nature Communications.

I thank the authors for their thorough and thoughtful response to my previous critique and appreciate the considerable effort they have devoted to strengthening the manuscript. The additional analyses addressing AR signaling, including the lack of correlation between AR activity and hypusination pathway gene expression, and the demonstration that eIF5Ahyp inhibition does not alter AR levels or activity, help to clarify the AR-independence of the hypusination axis. These additions enhance both the mechanistic depth and clinical relevance of the study. I appreciate the authors’ responsiveness and support the publication of the revised manuscript in Nature Communications. Further improvement in the quality of the western blot images would enhance the overall clarity and presentation of the findings.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Protein synthesis plays a central role in cancer development and progression. eukaryotic initiation factor 5A (eIF5A), a translation factor activated by hypusination, is implicated in tumorigenesis, however, its mode of action is still unclear. We find that hypusinated eIF5A (eIF5Ahyp) promotes metastasis and tumor growth in prostate cancer (PCa) by supporting mitochondrial metabolism and translation. eIF5Ahyp controls the subcellular localization of Mitochondrial Ribonuclease P Protein 3 (MRPP3) mRNA encoding a protein essential for mitochondrial tRNA (mt-tRNA) maturation. We show that eIF5Ahyp regulates the nuclear export of MRPP3 mRNA, its expression, thereby promoting mt-tRNA maturation. Our findings establish that MRPP3 enhances mitochondrial metabolism and supports PCa metastasis. Importantly, its expression restores mitochondrial translation and tumor growth inhibited by the downregulation of eIF5Ahyp. Together, we uncover a critical role for eIF5Ahyp in mitochondrial protein synthesis and highlight its broader implications in coordinating the expression of nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, linking hypusination to cancer progression.

---

## Introduction

Cancer cell growth and tumor progression are fundamentally driven by increased protein synthesis and metabolic reprogramming, two closely interconnected processes1. The translation factor eukaryotic initiation factor 5A (eIF5A) plays a crucial role in this context, being involved in the initiation, elongation and termination of translation for a specific subset of proteins2. There are two known highly homologous (91%) isoforms of eIF5A: eIF5A and eIF5A2 encoded by two different genes located on two different chromosomes. However, eIF5A2 expression is weak in the prostate 3. One of the defining features of both isoforms of eIF5A is that they undergo hypusination, a unique and highly conserved post-translational modification essential for its activity4. This modification, dependent on the polyamine spermidine, is catalyzed by two enzymes: deoxyhypusine synthase (DHPS) and the deoxyhypusine hydroxylase (DOHH).

Polyamines play an important role in cell proliferation, apoptosis, protein and nucleotide synthesis5. Previous studies, including our own, have demonstrated that polyamines are essential for metastasis in prostate cancer (PCa)6,7, and their levels are significantly elevated in PCa tissues compared to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) or normal prostate tissues7. These findings point to the polyamine/hypusination axis as a central player in PCa progression. Yet, despite the established link between hypusinated eIF5A (eIF5Ahyp) and neoplasia, the underpinning mechanisms of its pro-tumorigenic actions remained elusive. According to the GLOBOCAN study, PCa is the second most diagnosed cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer death among men worldwide 8. Removal of the prostate (prostatectomy) and radiotherapy are treatments for localized tumors. For more advanced PCa, anti-androgen treatments and/or chemotherapy (Docetaxel) are prescribed. However, patients quickly develop resistance, leading to fatal outcomes. Therefore, there is a critical need to discover therapies that target new molecular pathways.

Emerging evidence suggests that tumor cells hijack the translation machinery to selectively promote the expression of oncogenic proteins, thereby fueling cancer progression9. mRNA translation is an energy-intensive process, consuming 30 to 50% of the cell's energy, primarily supplied by mitochondria10. Recent evidence highlights eIF5A’s role in mitochondrial activity in macrophages polarization and senescence11,12. However, the implications of hypusination in mitochondrial metabolism in cancer progression have yet to be understood.

Mitochondria possess their own genome, consisting of 2 ribosomal RNAs, 22 tRNAs, and 13 encoding proteins which are essential components of the mitochondrial respiratory chain13. The genome is transcribed as a single polycistronic unit, requiring precise post-transcriptional modifications to generate functional and mature RNAs. These processes are controlled by nuclear-encoded proteins and require accurate coordination between the nuclear and mitochondrial genome to maintain mitochondrial function and integrity14. In this study, we show that eIF5Ahyp mediates the nuclear-mitochondrial dialogue by regulating the expression of the mitochondrial ribonuclease P protein 3 (MRPP3), a nuclear-encoded endonuclease essential for the maturation of mitochondrial tRNAs (mt-tRNA). Our data reveal that both eIF5Ahyp and its modifying enzyme DHPS are upregulated in PCa tumors, and elevated DHPS expression correlates with poor prognosis. Conversely, depletion of eIF5Ahyp suppresses PCa cell aggressiveness, reduces the growth of patient-derived tumoroids and limits metastasis in vivo. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that eIF5Ahyp regulates mitochondrial activity and the maturation of mt-tRNA through the downregulation of MRPP3. Consistent with the role of eIF5Ahyp, we identify MRPP3 as a pro-oncogenic factor that drives tumor growth and progression.

---

## Results

eIF5Ahyp and DHPS are upregulated in human PCa.
To determine the role of eIF5Ahyp in PCa, we carried out an in-depth bioinformatic analysis using several public RNA and proteomic databases and assessed hypusination in patient samples. Analysis of the CamCaP Study Group dataset (GSE70770)15, which includes benign and tumor tissues from 259 patients, revealed that the key regulators of hypusination: DHPS, DOHH, EIF5A and EIF5A2 were significantly overexpressed in tumor tissues compared to normal tissues (Fig. 1a,b). Consistent with the major role of polyamines in PCa, genes encoding enzymes involved in polyamine metabolism such as, the ornithine decarboxylase 1 (ODC1), spermidine synthase (SRM) and spermine synthase (SMS) were also significantly upregulated in tumors (Fig. 1a,b). We further analyzed the expression of DHPS, DOHH, EIF5A and EIF5A2 using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from Heidegger et al. 16. Integrated analysis of tumor and normal samples (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 1a-e) revealed a significant increase in the expression of EIF5A (p=6x10-5), DOHH (p=1.8x10-6), and DHPS (p<2.2x10-16) within tumoral epithelial cells compared to normal epithelial cells (Fig. 1d). Further analysis of four databases (TCGA, Grasso, Lapointe and Varambally) 17-19 showed a correlation between the expression of the genes of the hypusination module (eIF5A1, eIF5A2, DHPS and DOHH) (Supplementary Fig. 1f), however, only DHPS was consistently and significantly upregulated in PCa (Supplementary Fig.1h). Remarkably, patients with high levels of DHPS also showed significantly higher expression of DOHH and EIF5A (Supplementary Fig. 2e). These findings demonstrate that genes within the hypusination module—particularly DHPS—are upregulated in primary PCa.

Since PCa is dependent on androgens, expression analysis of the hypusination genes and AR was performed, but no significant correlation was found between hypusination genes and AR hallmark genes signature (Supplementary Fig.1g).

To determine if hypusination plays a role in PCa metastasis, we used Cancertool 20, a web-based platform for cancer gene expression analysis. DHPS was consistently overexpressed with the progression of the disease from primary tumors to metastases (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Fig.1h). Interestingly, our analysis of lymph node involvement (N) and distant metastasis (M), using the OncoDB online database, confirmed the rise in DHPS levels as the disease progressed (Fig. 1f,g and Supplementary Fig. 2a,b). We then analyzed the expression of the hypusination mRNAs in a database of metastatic castration prostate cancer patients (mCRPC), the most advanced form of PCa 21. Our results showed a significant increase in DHPS mRNA levels in neuroendocrine prostate cancer—a rare but highly aggressive subtype of PCa compared to adenocarcinoma—whereas DOHH, EIF5A, and EIF5A2 levels remained unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 2c). Finally, high DHPS mRNAs levels are associated with lower overall survival in prostate cancer patients based on the TCGA database (Supplementary Fig. 2d). All together, our data show that DHPS overexpression is associated with metastatic PCa and poor prognosis.

We then analyzed the protein levels of DHPS, DOHH, and eIF5A in a proteomic database that includes 306 patients with adenocarcinoma 22. Interestingly, the three proteins were significantly more expressed in tumoral than normal tissue (Supplementary Fig. 2f). To reinforce the relevance of our findings to human pathology, we assessed eIF5Ahyp, total eIF5A and DHPS protein levels by immunoblotting in the tumoral and adjacent normal tissues from PCa patients at our local hospital (CHU Nice) (Table 1 and Fig. 1h). Both eIF5Ahyp and DHPS were significantly elevated in tumors tissues (p = 0.0045 and p = 0.021, respectively) while eIF5A did not increase (Fig. 1i,j; Supplementary Fig. 2g). Similarly, we found that eIF5Ahyp, eIF5A and DHPS were significantly more expressed in PCa tumors than prostate tissue from patients with BPH (Supplementary Fig. 2h,i). Collectively, our results show that hypusination of eIF5A and DHPS levels were upregulated in PCa and associated with metastasis.

Inhibition of eIF5Ahyp suppresses tumor growth and PCa aggressiveness in different PCa models.
To characterize the pro-tumorigenic role of eiF5Ahyp in PCa, we employed two approaches to inhibit eIF5Ahyp: knockdown (KD) of DHPS using IPTG-inducible shRNA and pharmacological inhibition with GC7, a competitive inhibitor of DHPS, in three PCa cell lines (LNCaP, DU145 and PC3) (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Both DHPS knockdown and GC7 treatment led to significant reduction in cell proliferation, migration and invasion, as observed in Boyden chamber assays (Supplementary Fig. 3b,c). Notably, these interventions induced cell cycle arrest at the G0/G1 phase (Supplementary Fig. 3d) without causing apoptosis (Supplementary Fig. 3e).

To further validate these findings, we tested the effects of eIF5Ahyp inhibition on three patient-derived tumoroids (MSK-PCa1, MSK PCa3 and MSK-PCa4)23. We verified by cytometry and immunoblot that both GC7 and the downregulation of DHPS decreased eIF5Ahyp (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Fig. 3f,g) and observed that it induced a significant decrease in tumoroid growth as well as tumoroids formation capacities (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Fig. 4a). In contrast, GC7 had a minimal impact on the proliferation of organoids derived from normal prostate tissue (Supplementary Fig. 4b). To analyze the effects of the inhibition of eIF5Ahyp on cell division in 3D, we set up the fluorescence ubiquitin cell cycle indicator (FUCLCI)-based system in tumoroids. This technique allows the tracking of cell division in live cells within their endogenous environment with high spatiotemporal resolution24. We observed that GC7 treatment decreased cell division and increased cell cycle arrest within the 3D tumoroids (Fig. 2c). Additionally, GC7 significantly inhibited cell invasion, reducing the ability of tumoroid cells to migrate out of a soft collagen matrix by 60%, showing that eIF5Ahyp is associated with invasion in cancer cells (Fig. 2d).

We further evaluated the role of eIF5Ahyp in tumor growth in vivo using xenograft experiments. DU145 and PC3 cell lines, either expressing control shRNA (shCtl) or shDHPS, or treated with a vehicle or GC7 (10 mg/kg, i.p.), were implanted in mice. Both strategies with the two cell lines resulted in a significant reduction in tumor volume and weight (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 4c-f). These results were validated in RM-1 cells, a mouse prostate cancer cell line, injected subcutaneously in syngeneic C57Bl6J mice (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. 4g,h). Altogether, our data clearly show that eIF5Ahyp is required for PCa cell proliferation and tumor growth.

To determine the effects on metastasis, we used an orthotopic xenograft model in which PC3 cells expressing luciferase were injected directly into the prostate of mice, following established protocols25,26. This model allows the cancer cells to grow within their native microenvironment, enabling the development of primary tumors and the formation of distant metastases. The injected cells were either transfected with controls shRNA (shCtl) or shRNA targeting DHPS (shDHPS) to inhibit eIF5Ahyp. After 50 days, DHPS and eIF5Ahyp were significantly decreased in prostate tumors (Supplementary Fig. 4i) and tumor progression was assessed using the bioluminescent signal in animals. Remarkably, total luminescence was significantly reduced in mice injected with shDHPS cells, indicating lower tumor and metastasis burden (Fig. 2g). Further imaging of organs commonly invaded by metastatic cells (kidney, spleen, liver, lung and digestive track) revealed luminescent cells at distant sites, confirming metastatic spread (Supplementary Fig. 4j). While metastasis was observed in nearly all mice injected with shCtl cells, only 2 out of 7 mice injected with shDHPS cells developed metastases in the liver, spleen and kidney, and just 1 out of 7 showed metastatic spread to the digestive tract. Notably, none of the mice injected with shDHPS cells had lung metastases (Fig. 2h). Taken together, our results suggest that eIF5Ahyp is essential for promoting tumor growth and PCa metastasis.

eIF5Ahyp controls mitochondrial metabolism in PCa cells.
Building on previous studies linking eIF5Ahyp to mitochondrial metabolism11, we performed metabolite profiling of DHPS KD, GC7 treated cells and controls counterparts of DU145 cells. Of the 308 metabolites measured by LC-MS/MS, the steady-state levels of 71 metabolites showed significant changes in response to DHPS depletion (p<0.05) with six intermediates of the TCA cycle (citrate, aconitate, α-ketoglutarate, succinate, fumarate and malate) significantly decreased upon eIF5Ahyp inhibition (Fig. 3a, b and Table 2). Consistent with the metabolic effects of DHPS silencing, a reduction in TCA cycle intermediates was also confirmed in cells treated with GC7 (Supplementary Fig. 5a-d). To assess whether the activity of the TCA cycle was affected by eIF5Ahyp, we employed a stable isotope-tracing approach by using [13C ]-glucose (Fig. 3c). As expected, the inhibition of eIF5Ahyp, significatively decreased the abundance of aconitate (M+2), α-ketoglutarate (M+2), succinate (M+2), fumarate (M+2) and malate (M+2) in both cell lines with a more pronounced effect in DU145 (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 5e). Altogether, these results demonstrate that eIF5Ahyp maintains TCA cycle activity in PCa cells.

To determine if the decrease in eIF5Ahyp affects mitochondrial respiration, we measured the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) in PCa cells treated with GC7 or knockdown for DHPS. Although ECAR remained unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 5f,g), eIF5Ahyp inhibition impaired basal respiration, the maximum respiratory capacity and ATP production in DU145, LNCaP and PC3 cells (Fig. 3e, f, and Supplementary Fig.5h). Similar effects were observed in patient-derived tumoroids, where inhibition of eIF5Ahyp decreased OCR without significantly affecting ECAR (Supplementary Fig. 5i,j). Importantly, in line with our previous results showing that mitochondria adapt their shape and structure in response to energetic stress27, the effect of eIF5Ahyp inhibition were not due to a decrease in mitochondrial content (Supplementary Fig. 5k), but were associated with mitochondrial fragmentation and cristae disorganization; a hallmark of energetic stress28 (Fig. 3g,h).

In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that eIF5Ahyp is critical for maintaining mitochondrial metabolism and integrity in PCa cells.

eIF5Ahyp supports MRPP3 expression and mitochondrial t-RNA maturation.
Given the role of eIF5Ahyp in mRNA translation, we examined whether hypusination influences protein synthesis. Using a puromycin incorporation assay, we demonstrated that both GC7 and DHPS knockdown reduced the synthesis of nascent proteins in PCa cells and patient-derived tumoroids, indicating inhibited mRNA translation (Supplementary Fig. 6a-c). To further explore this, we conducted a polysome fractionation assay to examine the association of ribosomes with mRNA. Polysomes (actively translated mRNA, with two or more ribosomes, and monosomes, mRNA with one ribosome) were separated by zonal ultra-centrifugation on sucrose gradient according to their molecular weight and shape, and the different fractions were quantified as described previously29. We observed that GC7-treated cells exhibited a substantial decrease in polysomes and an increase in the 40S, 60S, and 80S ribosomal subunits, suggesting a global reduction in protein translation (Fig. 4a). A proteomic analysis identified significant downregulation of 439 proteins and upregulation of 85 proteins upon DHPS depletion in DU145 cells (Fig. 4b). Similar trends, with less protein affected, were seen in LNCaP cells, where 161 proteins were downregulated and 30 upregulated (Supplementary Fig. 6d).

Pathway enrichment analysis of the downregulated proteins highlighted disrupted mitochondrial translation and function as key processes affected by eIF5Ahyp depletion (Supplementary Fig. 6e). We performed polysome sequencing (Supplementary Fig.6f) and integrated the data with the proteomic study to identify common pathways using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA). We found that 26 pathways were commonly regulated (Fig. 4c). Notably, 11 of the top 15 pathways were associated with mitochondrial metabolism, including the mitochondrial protein-containing complex (Fig. 4d). To validate the role of hypusination in mitochondrial mRNA translation, we measured mitochondrial translation in cells treated with either vehicle, GC7, or chloramphenicol, a known inhibitor of mitochondrial protein synthesis. Consistent with chloramphenicol's effects, GC7 treatment significantly decreased mitochondrial translation (Supplementary Fig. 6g). Supporting these findings, data from the Heidegger single-cell RNA seq (scRNA-seq) patient database revealed a positive correlation between high DHPS and EIF5A expression and genes involved in mitochondrial translation in epithelial prostatic cells (Supplementary Fig. 6h-k). This establishes a clear link between eIF5Ahyp and mitochondrial translation. In agreement with these results, our proteomic analysis further identified the downregulation of the family of the Pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins in DU145 and LNCaP cells upon eIF5Ahyp depletion (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Fig. 6d). PPR proteins are essential RNA-binding proteins involved in mitochondrial RNA processing and translation30. Given its essential role as a regulator of mitochondrial RNA maturation and function, both in vitro and in vivo, MRPP3 emerged as a key target, 31,32. MRPP3 was one of the most significantly downregulated proteins following eIF5Ahyp inhibition, with a Log fold change of -2.99 in DU145 cells (Supplementary Fig. 7a).

Furthermore, we found that MRPP3 protein levels significantly correlate with the expression of DHPS, DOHH, eIF5A and A2 in the Sun proteomic database that includes 306 patients (Supplementary Fig. 7b). To confirm these findings, we validated the downregulation of MRPP3 protein levels in DU145, LNCaP and the three patient-derived tumoroids following GC7 treatment or DHPS KD (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 7c). To study the role of MRPP3 in the effects of eIF5Ahyp on mitochondrial translation, we overexpressed it in cells treated with GC7 (Supplementary Fig. 7d). Interestingly, elevated MRPP3 levels rescued the downregulation of mitochondrial translation induced by the inhibition of eIF5Ahyp (Fig. 4f) demonstrating that eIF5A regulates mitochondrial translation through MRPP3. To reinforce the link between eIF5Ahyp, MRPP3 and TCA cycle, we demonstrated that overexpression of MRPP3 partially reversed the inhibition of isocitrate Dehydrogenase (NAD(+)) 3 Catalytic Subunit Alpha (IDH3A), Succinate Dehydrogenase Complex Flavoprotein Subunit A (SDHA) and Dihydrolipoamide Dehydrogenase (DLD), three enzymes implicated in the regulation of the TCA cycle 11 (Fig. 4g).

MRPP3 functions as the catalytic enzyme of the RNaseP protein complex that regulates the maturation of mitochondrial tRNA (mt-tRNA)32 (Fig. 4h). To study the function of MRRP3 in the context of low hypusination level, the amount of immature tRNA was quantified in DU145 cells and tumoroids. Consistent with the decrease of MRPP3 caused by eIF5Ahyp inhibition, we observed a 2.7- and 8.2-fold increase in unprocessed mt-tRNAVal and mt-tRNAIle, respectively, following GC7 treatment (Fig. 4i). Additionally, we sorted dividing and arrested cells from FUCCI-expressing tumoroids (Fig. 2c) and quantified the relative amount of immature tRNA. Decreased Ki67 expression in GC7-treated and arrested cells confirmed their reduced proliferation (Supplementary Fig. 7e), and these cells also exhibited increased levels of immature mt-tRNAVal and mt-tRNAIle (Fig. 4j). To independently assess tRNA maturation, we analyzed pre-RNA cleavage by RNA-seq. A defect in the processing of mt-tRNA can be detected by the analysis of the reads in the region spanning the mitochondrial tRNA and mRNA sequences as previously described by Münch and Harper31. When tRNA processing is malfunctioning, sequence reads from the contiguous mRNA can extend into tRNA resulting in an increase of reads. Interestingly, we observed a significant increase in the reads spanning the regions between tRNA and ND2, COX1 and COX2 mRNA indicating an accumulation of immature mt-tRNA when eIF5A was inhibited (Fig. 4k). Altogether, our results show that eIF5Ahyp inhibition reduces MRPP3 expression and mt-tRNA maturation resulting in the decrease of mitochondrial translation.

eIF5Ahyp controls the nuclear export of MRPP3 mRNA.
We next aimed to investigate how hypusination regulates the expression of MRPP3. eIF5A is a nucleocytoplasmic shuttle protein and a RNA binding protein33,34. Furthermore, MRPP3 mRNA contains the sequence motif AAAUGU necessary for the binding to eIF5A as described by Xu et al.35. Thus, we postulated that eIF5A binds to MRPP3 mRNA and exports it to the cytosol to be translated. Using a RIP-qPCR assay we validated the binding of eIF5A to MRPP3 mRNA in DU145 and PC3 cells (Fig. 5a). In accordance with previous studies 36, we also showed that eIF5A binds to c-MYC mRNA but not RPLP0, GAPDH mRNA. Then, we examined whether hypusination interferes with the cellular localization of eIF5A in PCa cells by immunofluorescence. Similarly to our positive control leptomycin B, a potent inhibitor of nuclear export 37, the treatment with GC7 or the KD of DHPS significantly increased the amount of eIF5A in the nucleus compared to control cells (Fig. 5b,c). This result suggests, as previous described 38, that hypusination is required to target eIF5A in the cytoplasm. To demonstrate that eIF5A hypusination directly interferes with the transfer of MRPP3 mRNA in the cytosol, we performed cellular fractionation and quantified MRPP3 mRNA by q-PCR in the nuclear and cytosolic fractions of DU145 cells treated with GC7. To exclude an effect on the transcription of MRPP3, we first analyzed MRPP3 mRNA expression and showed that GC7 and leptomycin B did not affect MRPP3 mRNA levels (Fig. 5d). In accordance with the role of eIF5A in the nuclear-cytosolic transfer, GC7 led to the accumulation of MRPP3 and c-MYC mRNA in the nucleus whereas RPLP0 mRNA was not affected (Fig. 5e), showing that hypusination is required for the nuclear export of MRPP3 mRNA. Of note, leptomycin B increased MRPP3, RPLP0 and c-MYC mRNA in the nucleus and it also decreased the expression of MRPP3 and c-MYC, suggesting that nuclear export is a general mechanism that controls the expression of both proteins (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Importantly, we also observed that both immature mt-tRNAVal and mt-tRNAIle were significantly increased upon leptomycin B treatment (Supplementary Fig. 8b). Altogether, our results show that eIF5Ahyp regulates MRPP3 expression through the nuclear export of its mRNA.

MRPP3 is a pro-oncogenic protein that regulates mitochondrial function and PCa metastasis.
To investigate the role of MRPP3 in PCa cell metabolism and tumorigenesis, we generated DU145 and PC3 cell lines with stable knockdown of MRPP3 (shMRPP3) (Supplementary Fig. 9a) and conducted steady state metabolomics and Seahorse analysis to assess mitochondrial function. Similarly to the inhibition of eIF5Ahyp, the downregulation of MRPP3, significatively decreased the abundance of citrate (M+2), α-ketoglutarate (M+2), fumarate (M+2) and malate (M+2) (Fig. 6a, Supplementary Fig. 9b). In addition, silencing of MRPP3 decreased basal respiration, oxygen consumption, maximum respiratory capacities and ATP production in both cancer cell lines, indicating impaired mitochondrial function (Fig. 6b). Finally, downregulation of MRPP3 caused drastic changes in mitochondrial morphology, including increased circularity and disorganized cristae structure (Supplementary Fig. 9c, d). These findings establish MRPP3 as a central regulator of TCA cycle as well as mitochondrial activity and integrity in PCa cells.

Next, we examined whether the alterations of metabolism caused by MRPP3 silencing translated to changes in tumor growth and aggressiveness. In vitro, MRPP3 knockdown significantly reduced migration and invasion capabilities of PC3 and DU145 cells (Supplementary Fig. 9e). Consistent with these results, MRPP3 depletion led to a significant decrease in the growth of patient-derived tumoroids, highlighting its role in supporting tumor cell viability and expansion (Fig. 6c). To determine if MRPP3 has a pro-tumoral role in vivo, we performed subcutaneous injections of PCa cells. Remarkably, MRPP3 downregulation significantly decreased the tumor growth of both DU145 and PC3 in a xenograft model and RM-1 in syngeneic mice (Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Fig. 9f-h). Since MRPP3 expression rescued mitochondrial translation after the inhibition of eIF5Ahyp (Fig. 4f), we examined whether it could overcome the anti-migratory and anti-invasive effects of low eIF5Ahyp in vitro. Indeed, exogenous expression of MRPP3 restored the migratory and invasive capacities of DU145 treated with GC7 (Supplementary Fig. 9i,j). We next validated the contribution of MRPP3 in eIF5A effects in vivo. Notably, the expression of MRPP3 in DU145 cells, which have low levels of eIF5Ahyp, restored tumor growth in a xenograft model (Fig. 6f,g, Supplementary Fig. 10a). Similarly, MRPP3 overexpression counteracted partially the anti-tumoral effects resulting from the downregulation of DHPS in the RM-1 syngeneic model (Supplementary Fig. 10b-d) demonstrating that eIF5Ahyp plays a role in neoplasia through MRPP3. To further characterize the role of MRPP3 in PCa, we analyzed the formation of metastasis after injection of PC3-Luc cells expressing shMRPP3 in the prostate. Monitoring luminescence allowed us to track tumor spread, and inhibition of MRPP3 led to a significant reduction in total luminescence, indicating lower tumor burden (Fig. 6h). Moreover, metastasis analysis showed that only 1 out of 8 mice injected with cells depleted for MRPP3 developed metastases at two sites (spleen and digestive tract), while 100% control (shCtl)-injected mice exhibited widespread metastasis in the liver, spleen, and kidney (Fig. 6i, Supplementary Fig. 10e). To implement these results, MRPP3 expression was analyzed in clinical samples from our local cohort of PCa patients. MRPP3 was significantly upregulated in tumor tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues, further supporting its role as a pro-tumorigenic factor (Fig. 6j,k). Similarly, we found that MRPP3 is significantly more expressed in PCa tumors than prostate tissue from patients with Benign Prostate Hyperplasia (BPH) (Supplementary Fig. 10f). Interestingly, the analysis of Sun's proteomic database confirmed that MRPP3 is overexpressed in tumors 22 (Supplementary Fig. 10g). Of note, while we did not find a correlation between MRPP3 and DHPS or eIF5Ahyp in our cohort, Sun’s database revealed a correlation between the expression of MRPP3, DHPS, and eIF5A (Supplementary Fig. 7b).

In conclusion, our data demonstrate that MRPP3 is a protein driving the pro-oncogenic effects of eIF5A. It maintains mitochondrial function and controls tumor progression in PCa (Fig. 7). These findings highlight MRPP3 as a potential therapeutic target, with its inhibition offering a promising strategy to disrupt cancer cell metabolism and limit metastatic spread.
